parts.title: The postcard collector
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was nine, my aunt went to Norway and sent me a postcard of a red wooden boat. I put it on my bedroom wall, and a week later another one arrived from a friend of my mother's. By the end of that year, I had twelve, and I was hooked.

Today I have more than two thousand postcards, which I keep in shoeboxes under my bed. Many people think that collectors must be rich, but that is not true. Most of my cards cost less than a pound, and some were free. I find them in charity shops, at flea markets and in the boxes outside old bookshops. My favourite is a black-and-white card of a seaside town from 1932. On the back, a woman has written to her sister to say that the weather is terrible but the ice cream is excellent. I like to imagine who she was.

Of course, collecting has its problems. A few years ago, my brother borrowed some cards for a school project and returned them covered in glue. I was furious for a week. Since then, I have kept the best cards in plastic sleeves, and nobody is allowed to touch them without asking.

I am often asked what I will do with the collection one day. I have not decided yet. A museum might like some of the older cards, but I would rather give a few to my niece. She has just started school, and last week she sent me her first postcard. It shows a cat in a hat, and it is already my favourite.

questions.prompt: What made the writer start collecting postcards?
options: One that her aunt sent from another country
A present she bought on a school trip abroad
A picture she found in an old bookshop
questions.explanation: Her aunt sent a postcard of a red wooden boat from Norway, and others soon followed.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the cost of collecting?
options: It can be done without spending much
It costs more than most people expect
It depends on how old the cards are
questions.explanation: Most of her cards cost less than a pound and some were free.

questions.prompt: Why does she like the card from 1932?
options: It is the oldest card in her whole collection
The message makes her wonder about the sender
It shows the town where she was born
questions.explanation: The woman wrote about bad weather and good ice cream, and the writer likes to imagine who she was.

questions.prompt: How did she feel when her brother returned the cards?
options: Surprised that he had used them
questions.explanation: She says she was furious for a week.

questions.prompt: What does she say about the future of her collection?
options: She plans to sell the oldest cards
She will give all the cards to a museum
She has not made up her mind
questions.explanation: She says she has not decided yet and only mentions a few cards for her niece.

parts.title: Saturday with the model railway club
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every Saturday morning, a quiet room above the post office fills with the sound of tiny trains. It is the home of the Eastfield Model Railway Club, which has twenty members aged from eleven to eighty-three. [1] The layout took six years to finish, and it now covers most of the floor.

Club chairman Walter Frost says that the hobby is about much more than trains. 'People think it is only about buying engines,' he explains. [2] One member is a retired electrician who wires the lights, and another is a young art student who paints the tiny people.

New members usually begin with something simple. [3] Mr Frost remembers one boy who spent three weeks on a single signal box and then proudly showed it to everybody. 'That is the point,' he says. 'You learn patience.'

The club shows its layout to the public twice a year. [4] Last spring, more than four hundred visitors came, and the club made enough money to buy a new engine. [5] 'We have only one rule,' Mr Frost laughs. 'Nobody is allowed to play with the trains before they have helped to tidy the room.'
sentences: For example, they might paint a small station or glue together a bridge.
The atmosphere is friendly and relaxed, and new members are always welcome.
Together, they have built a model of a town, with hills, a river and more than fifty small buildings.
The oldest real station in the county closed more than forty years ago.
These open days are free, but visitors can give some money if they wish.
In fact, most members spend more time making scenery than running engines.

gaps.explanation: The first gap needs a sentence about what the members have built, because the next sentence says that the layout took six years.
This sentence explains that the hobby is more than engines, and it leads to the members who wire lights and paint people.
The sentence gives examples of simple jobs for beginners, before the story of the boy and his signal box.
The sentence explains that the open days are free and that visitors may give money, and the next sentence says how many came and how much money was made.
The sentence describes the friendly club, and the chairman then talks about its single rule.

parts.title: Better photos with a phone
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage:
Many people believe that they must [1] a lot of money on a camera before they can take good photographs, but this is not true. Most modern phones take excellent pictures, so the first thing to learn is how to [2] the best of what you already own. Start by looking carefully at the light. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times, because the sun is low and the colours are soft. Try to avoid the middle of the day, [3] the light is very strong.

Next, think about what is in the picture. Beginners often try to include too much. Move closer, or take a step to one side, [4] the picture looks simple and clear. If you are photographing people, ask them to forget about the camera and carry on [5] their normal conversation. These natural photos are usually much [6] interesting than posed ones.

Dear Rafe,
Thanks for your message! I am really pleased [1] you want to try rock climbing. I started last year, and it has become one [2] my favourite hobbies. The club meets every Wednesday evening, and it is easy to join. You just need to fill [3] a form and pay a small fee. The club will lend you a helmet and shoes, so you do not [4] to buy anything.

Most beginners are a little afraid at the start, but the teachers are very patient. If you feel nervous, they will climb with you [5] you feel confident. I will come along too, if you like. After the lesson, we usually have a hot drink in the café next door. Let me know [6] you would like to come on Wednesday.
Best wishes,

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: Today I'm talking to Callan Marsh, who has been making kites for thirty years. Callan, how did it all start?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: When I was eight, my grandfather took me to the beach with a kite he had made from newspaper and sticks. It flew badly, but I was fascinated. The next weekend I made my own.

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: Was it easy to learn?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: Not at all. My first ten kites crashed within a minute. But I read some old books at the library, and slowly I learned why the shape and the weight matter so much.

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: Where do you make them now?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: In the garage at home. I used to use the kitchen table until my wife asked me to stop, because there was paper and glue everywhere.

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: And do you sell them?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: Never. I give them to children at a local school, or I take a few to the festival every summer. If I started selling them, I think it would feel like work.

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: What's the biggest kite you've made?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: One that was six metres wide. It looked wonderful, but a sudden wind carried it into a tree, and I never got it back.

turns.speaker: nadine
turns.text: Finally, what would you say to someone who wants to start?

turns.speaker: callan
turns.text: Begin with a small, cheap kite, and don't expect it to be perfect. Fly it on a day with a steady wind, and you'll soon be hooked.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Do you think young people today have enough free time for hobbies? Why or why not?
Is it better to spend money on a hobby or to save it? Why?
What hobby would you like to try in the future, and why?
